query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy tantalum (Ta) with a lighter, but chemically similar, niobium (Nb) in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (i.e. developing a HfMoNbTiZr alloy) will reduce the overall density without substantially reducing the high yield strengths and ductility at both room and high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr, which exhibits a fine, predominantly BCC-based microstructure with a yield strength of about 1600 MPa at room temperature and ~855 MPa at elevated temperatures, but with a relatively high density of 10.21 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy’s composition by substituting Ta entirely with Nb, thereby forming a HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing should be conducted at room temperature and at 1000 °C under uniaxial tensile or compressive loading conditions that mimic service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention relies on the preservation of the beneficial BCC (and possibly ordered B2) microstructural features that underpin both high yield strength and ductility, while Nb’s similar chemical behavior compared to Ta supports comparable dislocation and precipitation strengthening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Because Nb has a significantly lower atomic density than Ta yet can promote similar interatomic bonding and phase stability, its substitution is expected to lower the overall alloy density. At the same time, if the microstructure (e.g. the formation of fine BCC/B2 phases) is preserved, the dislocation-related and precipitate-strengthening mechanisms responsible for high yield strength at room and elevated temperatures should remain active.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HfMoNbTiZr alloy should exhibit a density reduction on the order of 10–15% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining a yield strength in the range of approximately 1400–1600 MPa at room temperature and near 800–855 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature, and ~855 MPa yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Testing should replicate service-like conditions: static loading under uniaxial tension or compression at room temperature and at 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the complete substitution of Ta with Nb will preserve the precise balance of phase stability and strengthening; small shifts in phase fractions or microstructural features could lead to a modest reduction in yield strength. The quantitative impact on fracture toughness also needs to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same as-cast processing route as for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize its microstructure (via SEM/TEM and XRD), measure its density, and perform mechanical tests (yield strength and fracture toughness) at room temperature and 1000 °C. Compare these results with the baseline performance of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new alloy’s density reduction is less than approximately 10% relative to the baseline OR if its yield strengths at room temperature or at 1000 °C are reduced by more than 10% compared to HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis that substitution of Ta with Nb preserves the necessary mechanical performance while reducing density is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
